title: Lego Rail-Mounted Robot
description: Our group developed and programmed a Lego rail-mounted robot designed to transport a ball along a PVC pipe track, drop the object at the designated location, and autonomously return to its starting position using tape markers for navigation.

timeline.heading: Brainstorming
timeline.description: I proposed two designs: one with wheels holding PVC pipes from top and bottom, and another with four side wheels, a top brick, using a color sensor to detect colors. Clarence suggested a design with the baseplate on the top and a wheel on the bottom of the pipe to drive the robot, as well as a design with multiple side wheels for better stability. Jacob proposed a design with a wheel on the top of the pipe driving the robot. We compromised on a design with side wheels with the brick on top and the sensor underneath for reliable color detection.

timeline.heading: Task 1 - Robot
timeline.description:
Task 1 requires us to construct a robot that travels back and forth between the back tape on each end of the pipe while carrying a small mass. 

We built the robot by placing the brick on top, as well as the two small motors connected to the two axles that drive the four wheels. We designed our wheels to grip the side of the PVC pipe so that the corners of each wheel would contact the pipe. The sensor is on the bottom center of the robot, allowing for consistent color detection regardless of the direction it’s going in.

timeline.heading: Task 1 - Code
timeline.description: The robot goes straight until it detects the black tape at the end of the pipe, where the robot starts moving in the opposite direction. We did this by creating a speed variable that keeps track of the current direction of the robot with negative and positive signs indicating the direction. When the robot detects the black tape, we multiply the speed variable by -1 to change the direction of the robot. The robot stops checking the tape for 0.5 seconds after detecting the tape so it doesn’t immediately detect the black tape again and get stuck.

timeline.heading: Task 2 - Robot
timeline.description: For Task 2, we have to make the robot stop at a specified stopping color for 5 seconds. Afterward, the robot will continue going back and forth. For this task, we decided to change the underside of the robot to make it easier to remove the robot from the pipe. Also, when the robot was traveling along the pipe, the robot would flip over since the robot was top-heavy, so we decided to flip our robot upside down to stop the robot from flipping each time.

timeline.heading: Task 2 - Code
timeline.description: For task 2, we took the code from Task 1 and modified it for Task 2. First, we created a new variable, hasVisited, to keep track of whether the robot already stopped at the specified color. The variable is initially set to 0 to mark that it hasn’t visited the color. The robot moves forward until it detects the specified color. If the robot detects the specified color and hasVisited == 0, it stops and sets hasVisited to 1 to mark the robot has visited the color. Afterwards, the robot continues moving back and forth forever.

timeline.heading: Task 3
timeline.description:
For task 3, we were assigned a color pattern ( Blue / Yellow / Blue / Yellow / Green ) that our robot had to stop at in order.

 We took the code from Task 2 and changed hasVisited to keep track of the current stage the robot is in. For example, 0 marks no colors visited, 1 mark 1 color visited, 2 marks 2 colors visited, etc. We then set up an if statement checking if the robot is over the color in the current stage. If so, it stops for 5 seconds, increments hasVisited by 1, and resumes. Afterwards, we modified the code to incorporate function blocks to make the code cleaner.

timeline.heading: Task 4 - Robot
timeline.description:
For task 4, our robot now had to carry a ball to a specified color and drop the ball successfully into the receptacle. Our robot then has to return to the end wall, stopping between 5 - 20 cm from the wall using a distance sensor.

To accommodate for the ball, we added a ball holder connected to a motor that extends and retracts the holder to drop the ball. We also included a range sensor on the back to detect the distance to the wall.

resources.caption: Task 4 Robot Design with Ball Holder

timeline.heading: Task 4 - Code
timeline.description: We modified the code from Task 3 to stop at the specified color and execute a new function called DROP BALL that extends the bottom motors to drop the ball, then retracts it. Then, the robot continues to move until the range sensor reads 10cm from the wall.

timeline.heading: Task 5
timeline.description:
For Task 5, we had to make our robot travel the specified color pattern ( Blue / Yellow / Blue / Yellow / Green ) and drop the ball successfully into a box when it stops at a color for the second time. Afterward, the robot has to return to the end wall, stopping between 5-20 cm from the wall.

We modified the code from Task 3 to include the drop function. Then, we created three variables that keeps track of the number of times the robot visited a color. The forever loop continuously checks to see if it visited a color twice, drops the ball if so, and enters another forever loop inside the if statement. Inside this loop, the robot bounces back and forth until the distance sensor detects if the robot is close to the wall.

timeline.heading: Final Trial Run
timeline.description:
This project was a success as we successfully completed all the tasks and learned a lot about programming, teamwork, and problem-solving. As we progressed through each task, we adapted the code to work with the task at hand, such as making the robot move in a specific color pattern and dropping the ball when necessary. The use of variables, if statements, forever loops, and function blocks were crucial in making the code work.

Throughout this process, we not only improved our programming skills with Lego Mindstorm robots but also developed essential teamwork and problem-solving skills, as well as creativity in our brainstorming process. In hindsight, we could’ve made our design better by including customized parts, possibly 3D printed, to enhance the wheel grip on the PVC pipe. Overall, this project was an invaluable experience in designing robots that might be seen in an industrial setting.
